title: Your internet is underwater
text: The series you're streaming right now. The reels you scroll at 2am. Your tweets, your WhatsApp texts, this very page. You'd think they fly up to satellites and back. They don't. Almost everything you do online travels through physical cables lying on the ocean floor — these glowing threads. This is your internet.

title: The transatlantic highway
text: When you watch an American show from Europe, your click crosses the Atlantic through one of these cables and the video streams back — in about sixty milliseconds. Cables like MAREA move over 200 terabits every second. Millions of people's movies, calls and games, all inside a bundle of fibre thinner than your arm.

title: Egypt: the internet's chokepoint
text: Text someone in India from London, and your message almost certainly squeezes through here — the Suez Canal and the Red Sea. The shortest path between Europe and Asia funnels a huge share of the world's traffic across a few hundred kilometres of Egyptian desert. One anchor drag here, and half the world feels it.

title: 2Africa: the longest cable ever built
text: 45,000 kilometres — longer than a lap around the Earth. It rings the entire African continent, built by Meta, Vodafone, Orange and partners. When it's fully lit, three billion people's posts, payments and video calls will ride on this single loop.

title: Big Tech lays its own
text: Every photo you put on Instagram, every search you type — Google, Meta, Microsoft and Amazon used to rent the pipes that carry them. Not anymore. Now they lay their own cables across entire oceans. Most new transoceanic fibre today is funded by the same companies whose apps fill your home screen.

title: A single thread: Tonga
text: Now imagine your whole country hanging from one cable. That's Tonga. When a volcano erupted under the Pacific in 2022, it snapped their only link — and one hundred thousand people simply went offline. No banking, no news, no calls home. For five weeks, until a single ship found the cable and spliced it back together.

title: Watch it grow: 1989 to today
text: In 1989 there were just a handful of fibre systems. Then email. Then the web. Then video, then streaming, then AI. Watch four decades of the internet physically wiring itself around the planet, cable by cable, all the way to the routes planned for 2029.

title: Now explore
text: So next time a reel loads instantly, remember — it probably crossed an ocean to reach you. Click any cable to see who built it. Click a landing station. Search your country. Scrub the timeline. Everything here is real, current data. Go find the cable your internet rides on.
